full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionTo address the ongoing threat of influenza, the WHO, through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS), annually recommends vaccine strains in September for the Southern Hemisphere and in February for the Northern Hemisphere. However, due to the rapid antigenic evolution of influenza viruses, vaccine–strain mismatches are common (Heikkinen et al., 2014). Therefore, both production speed and breadth of protection offered by the next generation of influenza vaccines must be improved (CIDRAP, 2025).In our previous study, we demonstrated that a T214A mutation in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein of the influenza B virus significantly impaired its cross-protection. This finding led us to propose a strategy based on minimal antigenic modification to enhance the breadth of cross-neutralization of influenza B vaccines without compromising their antigenic integrity.The influenza B virus has four recognized major antigenic regions on HA: the 120-loop, 150-loop, 160-loop, and the 190-helix (Wang et al., 2008). Notably, the 190-helix, which forms part of the receptor-binding site, is one of the most immunologically significant regions, and contains a potential N-linked glycosylation site (Skehel and Wiley, 2000; Schulze, 1997). In our previous study of SARS-CoV-2, we showed that substitutions at spike glycosylation sites can alter sensitivity to antibody-mediated neutralization (Li et al., 2020). Previous studies have explored glycosylation engineering as an approach to improving influenza vaccine immunogenicity and cross-protection (Hu et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2010; Tseng et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020).In the present study, BW06 showed more balanced and more broadly neutralizing activity than BV21 against pseudoviruses representing multiple influenza B subclades. In contrast, BV21 showed potent neutralization activities primarily against the V1A.3a.2 subclade, but much weaker activity against other subclades. Moreover, the D212N substitution in the BV21 background enhanced cross-neutralizing responses and improved protection against selected heterologous strains in mice. Previous studies have highlighted the influence of B-cell competition on antibody responses to conserved epitopes (Dosenovic et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020). Glycan recognition by mannose-binding (MBL) lectin may also influence interactions between antigens and the innate immune system (Ip et al., 2009). The potential involvement of germinal center competition and MBL-mediated antigen clearance in the responses observed here remains hypothetical, as neither mechanism was examined in this study. Glycan engineering has been explored as a means of directing antibody responses toward conserved regions in other vaccine settings (Eggink et al., 2014). However, the present study did not determine whether the increased breadth involved altered epitope targeting.This study evaluated vaccine immunogenicity at matched mRNA doses, with cell-based assays used to confirm antigen expression. These comparisons assess immunogenicity under the tested conditions but do not isolate the potential contributions of differences in antigen abundance or trimer stability. Furthermore, because D212N changes both the amino acid side chain and the glycosylation status, the specific contribution of the added glycan remains unresolved. Future studies incorporating ferret models and sera from individuals with prior influenza infection or vaccination could further assess antigenic breadth and the influence of pre-existing immunity.In conclusion, the D212N-modified BV21 mRNA vaccine enhanced cross-neutralizing responses against the tested B/Victoria-lineage viruses, while the observed survival benefit was specific to the high-dose group challenged with B/Washington/02/2019. When monitoring the prevalence of viral strains, it is noteworthy that our updated sequence analysis revealed a renewed increase in the proportion of N212 after 2024, highlighting the continued relevance of N212 among circulating influenza B viruses. These findings support further exploration of glycosylation-site engineering as a strategy to broaden influenza B vaccine protection.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInfluenza is an acute respiratory infection that remains a major global health challenge, with severe respiratory symptoms and widespread seasonal outbreaks (Briand et al., 2011; Keech and Beardsworth, 2008). According to the World Health Organization (WHO), influenza is responsible for approximately 3–5 million cases of severe illness and 290,000–650,000 respiratory-related deaths annually (WHO, 2025). Influenza B virus, together with influenza A, is one of the most prevalent pathogens in humans, causing epidemics every 2–4 years. Its high intrinsic mutation rate, coupled to seasonal surges during winter and spring, complicates timely vaccine updates. Therefore, influenza B imposes a significant burden on public health systems and has substantial economic consequences worldwide. Although neuraminidase inhibitors and baloxavir have activity against influenza B viruses, vaccination remains the primary preventive strategy.Conventional influenza vaccines, including inactivated and live-attenuated formulations, function primarily through the induction of neutralizing antibodies and the stimulation of cellular immune responses. However, these traditional approaches often struggle to keep pace with the virus's rapid antigenic drift, leading to frequent mismatches between vaccine strains and the circulating viruses (Jin and Chen, 2014; Wu et al., 2024). Such mismatches can markedly reduce vaccine efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for next-generation vaccines that can be produced rapidly and provide broad cross-protection against diverse influenza variants.mRNA-based vaccines offer a promising alternative due to their rapid and scalable manufacturing process and their efficacy in inducing protective immunity (Schmid, 2024; Hu et al., 2024). Notably, mRNA vaccine production is largely sequence-independent, allowing its swift adaptation to emerging viral strains—an advantage over peptide- or DNA-based platforms (WHO, 2021). In a previous study, we observed that the T214A mutation in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein significantly affected the cross-neutralizing activity of influenza B vaccines, which we suggested might involve alterations in their glycosylation patterns (Cheng et al., 2025). We also noted that the recently WHO-recommended vaccine strain B/Austria/1359417/2021 (BV21) has a threonine at position 214 but differs from the broadly reactive strain B/Wyoming/06/2014 (BW06) at position 212, where it has an aspartic acid (D) rather than an asparagine (N). Because position 212 may also influence glycosylation, we hypothesized that the D212N substitution could broaden the antibody response elicited by BV21, potentially through altered HA glycosylation.In this study, we designed mRNA-based vaccine constructs encoding the HA proteins of either BW06 or BV21 and introduced the D212N mutation into the BV21 background. title: Spatial risk factors associated with outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza in Pennsylvania’s commercial poultry farms
abstract: A retrospective case-control study was constructed to identify risk factors associated with outbreaks of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in Pennsylvania's commercial poultry industry. Eligible farms were stratified by outbreak status and randomly allocated to a model development dataset (60%) and an independent model testing dataset (40%). GIS-derived exposure variables were screened for associations with HPAI infection in the model development dataset. Subsequent multivariable logistic regression identified duck capacity density (OR: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.03-1.10), road density (OR: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.01-1.12), and freshwater pond abundance (OR: 1.05, 95% CI: 1.02-1.08) as factors associated with increased risk of HPAI. In contrast, higher elevation (OR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81-0.96) was associated with reduced risk. Duck (OR: 13.05, 95% CI: 5.00-34.04), layer (OR: 3.19, 95% CI: 1.24-8.23), miscellaneous (OR: 5.76, 95% CI: 1.62-20.42), mixed-species (OR: 13.68, 95% CI: 5.04-37.10), and turkey (OR: 9.46, 95% CI: 3.49-25.67) farms exhibited higher odds of infection relative to broiler reference farms. The model demonstrated good discrimination in the development dataset (AUC = 0.8542) and in the testing dataset (AUC = 0.8605). In testing, sensitivity was 78.1% and specificity was 78.9%. Global Moran's I indicated reduced spatial autocorrelation following model fitting, although significant residual spatial autocorrelation remained. The findings demonstrate that confirmed HPAI outbreaks were associated with farm-level characteristics and spatial variables representing wild bird ecology, environmental conditions, and poultry industry dynamics. Integrating farm-level surveillance with environmental and poultry industry spatial data provides a practical framework for HPAI risk and targeted disease control.
